newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany to award public phone licences.
newsitem.headline: Germany to award public phone licences.

text.p: Germany could award the first licences for public phone services as early as this week, kicking off the final phase of full deregulation of telecommunications planned for 1998.

German Post and Telecommunications Minister Wolfgang Boetsch told reporters late on Tuesday there were currently 11 applications for licences to provide public telephone services, now a monopoly service of Deutsche Telekom.

Boetsch said he wanted to give the companies applying for the licences more planning security in the run-up to 1998 by awarding the licences before the end of the year. Seven of the applications are for a national telephone service.
"The licences could be awarded this week. It depends on how fast we can work through the applications," a spokesman for the minister told Reuters on Wednesday.

Next year will see some of the world's largest players on the telecommunications market and their German partners, several of Germany's biggest enterprises, make their final moves to compete against monopoly Telekom beginning in 1998.
Public voice telephone services is the last stone in Telekom's fortress that has kept competition out of a market expected to be worth more than 100 billion marks ($64.5 billion) by the year 2000.

Industry representatives have criticised the licencing procedure ahead of the government's decision. Some companies have complained that government plans to charge a fee of 40 million marks for a licence for national coverage put up stiff barriers for newcomers hoping to compete against Telekom.

But Boetsch rejected such criticism. He said the fees were studied by a joint committee of the post, economics and finance ministries and that while Germany would impose a one-off fee, it was typical in other countries to raise an annual levy.
"I don't see any barriers to entering the market," he said.
In addition to national licence applications, there were four applications for public phone licences for regional services. These would carry lower fees.
The fees will be based on a per capita charge of around 50 pfennigs per resident, with some adjustments for high-traffic business centres where few people live.
The German government, searching for ways to stop yawning budget deficits, hopes to gain around 1.6 billion marks in fees for new telecommunications licences.
Industry representatives have called this an "investment tax" that would become just another excuse not to invest in Germany. ($ = 1.550 German Marks)
